Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
The world is a dangerous place
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence in this profile. It is much more characteristic of sexual trauma or interpersonal violation with a strong disgust/shame component, and here there are no supporting memory, trigger, threat, or strategy items that would make this appraisal clinically coherent. The remaining items describe intrusive, alien, uncontrolled traumatic memory and general danger/body-reactivity beliefs, which fit severe PTSD, but the contamination item stands out as a trauma-incongruent appraisal.

vignette: Mara, a 28‑year‑old European police officer, was 45 minutes into a night patrol when the call that would change her life came in. A 23‑year‑old man had been found in a parked car with a weapon, and the squad had already been dispatched. Mara arrived to find the suspect unresponsive, and another officer had already fired a warning shot into the air. The shot rang out, the sound a harsh, metallic clang that seemed to reverberate into Mara’s bones. The man did not die immediately, but he was later pronounced dead, and a coroner ruled the fatal shot had come from the other officer’s gun. The scene left Mara shaking; her hands had clenched around her radio as she watched the suspect’s body go still. She felt a pang of betrayal—someone she had sworn to protect had, in a split second, turned weapon against a fellow officer. In the weeks that followed, the memory of that night did not stay buried. Whenever the hum of a police radio or the distant echo of a siren rose, Mara found herself transported back to the fluorescent glare of the victim’s empty chest and the crack of gunfire. The recollection was not a distant flash; the sights, the sharp, acrid smell of gunpowder, the trembling of the suspect’s hands—it all flooded her senses simultaneously, as if the scene were happening again. Yet the memory felt oddly foreign, as though it belonged to another person, and she could not tell when she was looking at it and when it was looking at her. It burst into her mind at the most inconvenient times, forcing her to stare at the ceiling or to clutch her chest until the pulse in her ears subsided. She could not control when it would surface, and each intrusion felt as if it were a separate entity, a ghost of a night that was neither hers nor wholly remote. Mara’s body had come to respond as though danger were ever present. Even when she sat on the front bench of a grocery store, her shoulders tense, her heart racing, she could not shake the feeling that someone was watching. She started to believe that the world itself was hostile, that danger could erupt from any stranger’s face. The betrayal she felt at the time of the shooting amplified these fears; she was convinced that someone she had trusted had turned on her. The conviction that the world was dangerous made her hyper‑vigilant: a sudden shout from a passing cyclist would feel like a threat, a shadow in the parking lot a possible attacker. Her negative appraisals, therefore, set the stage for her memories to intrude. In any setting where a siren wailed or a bright flash startled her, her mind could not resist the lure of the night’s trauma. The belief that danger lurked in the ordinary became a trigger that pulled the intrusive memory out of its hidden place and into her present consciousness. This loop of appraisals and memory intrusions tightened the longer she avoided confronting the experience. The intrusive memories, in turn, reinforced Mara’s negative appraisals. Each time the image of the gunshot re‑ignited, her heart hammered, her muscles tensed, and she felt her world shrink to a single point of potential threat. She began to think that she was no longer safe even in the most mundane places. The memory’s full sensory fidelity—seeing the man’s pale face, hearing the crack of the gun, feeling the cold air of the station—made her believe that the same scene could repeat itself. She started to doubt her own judgment: “If I can’t trust my senses to tell me I’m safe, how can I trust my body?” The memory thus kept the sense of danger alive, and she became convinced that betrayal had once again taken root in her life. When the pattern of avoidance grew, the impact on her job and her personal life became undeniable. Mara began arriving late to shifts, hoping to avoid any situation that might bring the memory to the surface. Her partner began to notice her growing reluctance to engage in patrol duties, and the couple she shared a home with expressed concern over the increasing distance between them. Her supervisor requested that she attend a safety training session on stress management, but Mara declined, fearing that the discussion would trigger her memories and prove her world still as dangerous as ever. The sense that the world was hostile made her doubt whether she could ever be at peace, both at work and at home. Today, Mara is finally seeking help because each day she wakes with a pulse racing, unable to focus on her own children’s homework or on the hum of the city outside her window. She fears that she will lose her job, lose the trust of those she loves, and that the memory will keep haunting her until she can no longer hold her job as a police officer. She hopes that by facing the trauma she can regain control of her body’s reactions, feel safe again in her everyday life, and reconcile the betrayal she experienced with the role she loves.
